extracted.intended_audience: graduate or advanced undergraduate students studying algebraic topology; instructors and researchers needing reference material on cohomology and Poincaré duality
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and precise statements about cup products, realizability of polynomial/truncated polynomial cohomology rings, orientations of manifolds, fundamental classes, and Poincaré duality, with examples and exercises. Targeted at readers learning or applying these concepts in algebraic topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realizability of polynomial cohomology R[α] (even d)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each even d there exists a CW complex X_d which is simultaneously an example for all the admissible choices of coefficients R in the table. X_d can be chosen to have the simplest CW structure consistent with its cohomology, namely a single cell in each dimension a multiple of d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: X_2 = CP^∞, X_4 = HP^∞. For X_6 one gets H^*(X_6; Z_p) ≈ Z_p[α] for primes p = 7,13,19,31,... (primes of the form 3s+1). In terms of Z coefficients, if α generates H^d(X_d; Z), each power α^i is an integer a_i times a generator of H^{di}(X_d; Z); a_i ≠ 0 if H^*(X_d; Q) ≈ Q[α], and a_i relatively prime to p if H^*(X_d; Z_p) ≈ Z_p[α]. Constructions referenced in [SSAT] and [Hoffman & Porter 1973].

rubrics_metrics.name: Realizability of truncated polynomial rings R[α]/(α^{n+1})
rubrics_metrics.description: Truncated polynomial rings R[α]/(α^{n+1}) can be realized (examples: RP^n, CP^n, HP^n), leaving aside the trivial n = 1 case where spheres provide examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The same analysis as for full polynomial rings largely settles which truncated polynomial rings are realizable; there are only a few more than for full polynomial rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product closure for polynomial cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: If two spaces have polynomial cohomology (with finitely many polynomial generators in each dimension), then their product has polynomial cohomology equal to the tensor product: R[α_1,...,α_m] ⊗_R R[β_1,...,β_n] = R[α_1,...,α_m,β_1,...,β_n].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: (CP^∞)^n has H^*( (CP^∞)^n; Z ) ≈ Z[α_1,...,α_n] with each α_i 2-dimensional. However, for Z and Z_p coefficients, products of one-variable examples do not exhaust all possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realization with Q coefficients via J(S^{d_i})
rubrics_metrics.description: The spaces J(S^{d_i}) realize all choices of even d_i's with Q coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus for rational coefficients, product constructions and these J(S^{d_i}) spaces cover realizability of polynomial algebras with specified even-degree generators.

rubrics_metrics.name: BU(n) / Grassmannian criterion (Z-coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Grassmann manifold G_n(C^∞) (also BU(n)) has H^*(G_n(C^∞); Z) ≈ Z[α_1,...,α_n] with |α_i| = 2i; it provides realizations of polynomial algebras with generators in specified even degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BU(n) is the classifying space for U(n) and is central to vector bundle and K-theory constructions; it is one of the basic non-product examples over Z coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSp(n) / quaternionic Grassmannian criterion (Z-coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quaternionic Grassmann manifold G_n(H^∞) (also BSp(n)) has H^*(G_n(H^∞); Z) ≈ Z[α_1,...,α_n] with |α_i| = 4i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides polynomial cohomology examples with generators in degrees multiples of 4; another basic classifying-space example over Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: BSU(n) criterion (Z-coefficients)
rubrics_metrics.description: The classifying space BSU(n) has cohomology the same as BU(n) but with the first generator α_1 omitted, so H^*(BSU(n); Z) ≈ Z[α_2,...,α_n] with |α_i| = 2i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives realizations of polynomial rings missing low-degree generator(s); part of the classification of realizable polynomial cup-product rings over Z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification (Andersen & Grodal 2008) for Z-coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: The listed examples (products of one-variable examples, BU(n), BSp(n), BSU(n) and their products) account for all the realizable polynomial cup-product rings with Z coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Z_p coefficient case is more complicated and treated separately (reference §3.G).

rubrics_metrics.name: Free graded commutative algebra characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: A free graded commutative algebra is a tensor product of single-generator free graded commutative algebras; the single-generator free ones are either polynomial algebras R[α] on even-dimensional generators α or quotients R[α]/(2α^2) with α odd-dimensional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If R is a field, R[α]/(2α^2) reduces to the exterior algebra R[α] when char R ≠ 2, or to the polynomial algebra R[α] when char R = 2. Every graded commutative algebra is a quotient of a free one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subcomplexes of T^n produce quotient-cohomology by monomial ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: For T^n with standard cell structure, H^*(T^n; Z) is the exterior algebra Z[α_1,...,α_n] and for a subcomplex X ⊂ T^n obtained by omitting cells, H^*(X; Z) is the quotient of Z[α_1,...,α_n] obtained by setting monomials corresponding to omitted cells equal to zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deleting a certain 3-cell from T^3 yields H^*(X; Z) ≈ Z[α_1,α_2,α_3]/(α_2 α_3). More generally these cohomology rings are polynomial rings modulo ideals generated by monomials, and the ring determines the subcomplex up to permutation of circle factors (Gubeladze 1998).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cohen–Macaulay cohomology-ring criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A Cohen–Macaulay (CM) ring example: X = CP^∞/CP^{n−1} has H^*(X; Z) embedded in Z[α] as the subring generated by 1, α^n, α^{n+1}, ...; as a module over Z[α^n] it is free with basis {1, α^{n+1}, ..., α^{2n−1}}, so H^*(X; Z) is CM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition used: a ring containing a polynomial subring over which it is a finitely generated free module. CM cup-product rings occur more frequently than full polynomial rings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing of cup products for unions of contractible opens
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is the union of contractible open subsets A and B, then all cup products of positive-dimensional classes in H^*(X; R) are zero. Generalization: if X is union of n contractible open subsets, all n-fold cup products of positive-dimensional classes are zero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies in particular to suspensions. Use the relative cup product H^k(X,A;R) × H^ℓ(X,B;R) → H^{k+ℓ}(X, A∪B; R) to show vanishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obstruction for maps between projective spaces via cup product
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no map RP^n → RP^m inducing a nontrivial map H^1(RP^m; Z_2) → H^1(RP^n; Z_2) if n > m; analogous statement for CP^n → CP^m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from cup-product considerations; used in applications such as proofs of Borsuk–Ulam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lefschetz fixed-point application via cohomology ring homomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the Lefschetz fixed point theorem and the fact that f^*: H^*(CP^n; Z) → H^*(CP^n; Z) is a ring homomorphism, every map f: CP^n → CP^n has a fixed point if n is even; when n is odd there is a fixed point unless f^*(α) = −α for generator α ∈ H^2(CP^n; Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibit exceptional maps in odd n case (see referenced Exercise in §2.C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finite-generation hypothesis for Künneth/cross-product is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The cross product map H^*(X; Z) ⊗ H^*(Y; Z) → H^*(X × Y; Z) need not be an isomorphism if X and Y are infinite discrete sets; finite generation hypothesis in Theorem 3.15 is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that algebraic hypotheses (finite generation in each degree) cannot be omitted in Künneth-style theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Z-to-Z_p determination when H_n(X; Z) free
rubrics_metrics.description: If H_n(X; Z) is free for each n, then H^*(X; Z_p) and H^*(X; Z) ⊗ Z_p are isomorphic as rings; in particular the ring structure with Z coefficients determines the ring structure with Z_p coefficients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use universal coefficient and reduction mod p arguments; warns that Z-cohomology can determine mod-p cohomology under freeness hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat: Z-cohomology can fail to determine Z_p-cohomology
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples exist (exercise 8) of spaces X and Y with same Z-cohomology rings but different Z_p-cohomology rings, showing Z-cohomology may not determine Z_p information in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct spaces with same 3-skeleton but different 4-cell attachments to produce same Z but different Z_p cohomology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of manifold via local homology
rubrics_metrics.description: An n-manifold M is a Hausdorff space where each point has a neighborhood homeomorphic to R^n; equivalently characterized by local homology: H_i(M, M−{x}; Z) is nonzero only for i = n, and equals H_{n−1}(S^{n−1}; Z).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compact n-manifold is called 'closed'. Examples: S^n, RP^n, CP^n, lens spaces; product of closed manifolds is closed manifold of summed dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poincaré duality (primitive form) for closed orientable manifolds
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed orientable n-manifold M there are isomorphisms H^k(M; Z) ≈ H^{n−k}(M; Z) for all k (with cohomology groups in negative dimension taken to be zero). Without orientability, H^k(M; Z_2) ≈ H^{n−k}(M; Z_2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Via universal coefficient theorem one obtains corresponding statements about homology up to torsion. Poincaré duality reflects symmetry in homology and is tied to existence of a fundamental class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of local and global orientations
rubrics_metrics.description: A local orientation at x is a choice of generator of H_n(M, M−{x}; Z). An orientation of M is a function x ↦ µ_x assigning to each x a local orientation µ_x ∈ H_n(M || x) satisfying a local consistency condition: each x has a neighborhood B for which all µ_y (y ∈ B) are images of one generator µ_B ∈ H_n(M || B). If such an orientation exists, M is orientable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This algebraic-topological definition captures the usual geometric notion: rotations preserve and reflections reverse the chosen generator. The same notion generalizes by replacing Z with any commutative ring R; an R-orientation requires generators that are units in R.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between orientability and orientation-covering
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a two-sheeted covering space M whose points are local orientations µ_x; for connected M, M is orientable iff M has two components. More generally, M is orientable if π_1(M) has no subgroup of index two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The covering M→M encodes orientation choices; connectedness properties of the cover characterize orientability. Every manifold has an orientable two-sheeted cover.

rubrics_metrics.name: R-orientability criterion via units of R
rubrics_metrics.description: A manifold is R-orientable iff it admits a section of the covering MR→M whose values at points are generators of H_n(M || x; R) ≈ R (i.e., units in R). If R has an element of order two (equivalently 2=0 in R), a nonorientable M may be R-orientable; in particular every manifold is Z_2-orientable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus orientability depends on coefficient ring R; orientability over Z implies orientability over every R, while nonorientable manifolds are R-orientable exactly when R admits a unit of order two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence and characterization of fundamental class
rubrics_metrics.description: An element µ ∈ H_n(M; R) whose image in H_n(M || x; R) is a generator for all x is called a fundamental class for M with coefficients in R. For closed M a fundamental class exists iff M is R-orientable; conversely a fundamental class implies compactness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The map H_n(M; R) → H_n(M || x; R) plays central role; a fundamental class provides an R-orientation and is also called an orientation class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 3.26 (structure of top homology groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) If M is R-orientable, H_n(M; R)→H_n(M || x; R) ≈ R is an isomorphism for all x∈M. (b) If M is not R-orientable, the map is injective with image { r ∈ R | 2r = 0 } for all x. (c) H_i(M; R)=0 for i>n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: H_n(M; Z) is Z if M orientable and 0 otherwise; H_n(M; Z_2)=Z_2 in either case. The proof uses Lemma 3.27 and analysis of sections of MR→M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 3.27 (local-to-global extension for compact subsets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let M be n-manifold and A⊂M compact. (a) If x↦α_x is a section of MR→M then there is a unique class α_A ∈ H_n(M || A; R) whose image in H_n(M || x; R) is α_x for all x ∈ A. (b) H_i(M || A; R)=0 for i>n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This lemma underlies uniqueness/existence of orientation classes over compact subsets and is proved by Mayer–Vietoris reductions, convex-ball arguments, and excision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicial/cellular criterion for fundamental class
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed n-manifold with simplicial structure, a fundamental class in simplicial homology can be represented by a sum ∑ k_i σ_i of n-simplices where each coefficient k_i is ±1 and sign choices must make the sum a cycle; such a choice of signs is possible iff M is orientable. With Z_2 coefficients, ∑ σ_i always defines a fundamental class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a CW decomposition with a single n-cell: if M orientable the cellular boundary map is zero and H_{n−1}(M; Z) is free; if nonorientable the boundary sends generator to twice a generator producing Z_2 torsion in H_{n−1}(M; Z).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 3.28 (torsion in H_{n−1})
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is a closed connected n-manifold, the torsion subgroup of H_{n−1}(M; Z) is trivial if M is orientable and Z_2 if M is nonorientable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses universal coefficient theorem and sizes of H_n(M; Z_p) for primes p.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition 3.29 (vanishing for noncompact manifolds)
rubrics_metrics.description: If M is a connected noncompact n-manifold, then H_i(M; R) = 0 for i ≥ n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: represent classes by cycles with compact image, place them in complements of compact sets and apply Lemma 3.27; for i=n sections on MR must vanish because of noncompactness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and chain-level formula for cap product
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an R-bilinear cap product C_k(X; R) × C^ℓ(X; R) → C_{k−ℓ}(X; R) for k ≥ ℓ defined on a singular simplex σ: Δ^k→X and ϕ ∈ C^ℓ(X; R) by σ ∩ ϕ = ϕ(σ|[v_0,...,v_ℓ]) · σ|[v_ℓ,...,v_k].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This induces cap product on homology/cohomology and satisfies ∂(σ ∩ ϕ) = (−1)^ℓ(∂σ ∩ ϕ − σ ∩ δϕ). Cap product provides the algebraic mechanism for Poincaré duality isomorphisms.
